original_value: One important objective of urban traffic signal control is to reduce individual delay and improve safety for travelers in both private car and public bus transit. To achieve signal control optimization from the perspective of all users, this paper proposes a platoon-based adaptive signal control (PASC) strategy to provide multimodal signal control based on the online connected vehicle (CV) information. By introducing unified phase precedence constraints, PASC strategy is not restricted by fixed cycle length and offsets. A mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model is proposed to optimize signal timings in a real-time manner, with platoon arrival and discharge dynamics at stop line modeled as constraints. Based on the individual passenger occupancy, the objective function aims at minimizing total personal delay for both buses and automobiles. With the communication between signals, PASC achieves to provide implicit coordination for the signalized arterials. Simulation results by VISSIM microsimulation indicate that PASC model successfully reduces around 40% bus passenger delay and 10% automobile delay, respectively, compared with signal timings optimized by SYNCHRO. Results from sensitivity analysis demonstrate that the model performance is not sensitive to the number fluctuation of bus passengers, and the requested CV penetration rate range is around 20% for the implementation.

result.paraphrase: An important goal of urban traffic signal control is to cut individual delay and enhance safety for travelers in private cars and public bus transit alike. To optimize signals from all users’ perspective, this paper presents a platoon-based adaptive signal control (PASC) approach that uses online connected vehicle (CV) information to support multimodal signal control. By adding unified phase precedence constraints, the PASC strategy is not limited by a fixed cycle length or offsets. A mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model is introduced to optimize signal timing in real time, with platoon arrival and discharge dynamics at the stop line represented as constraints. Using passenger occupancy at the individual level, the objective function seeks to minimize total personal delay for both buses and automobiles. Through communication among signals, PASC provides implicit coordination for signalized arterials. VISSIM microsimulation results show that the PASC model reduces bus passenger delay by about 40% and automobile delay by about 10% compared with signal timings optimized by SYNCHRO. Sensitivity analysis indicates that model performance is not sensitive to fluctuations in the number of bus passengers, and the required CV penetration rate for implementation is about 20%.
